stem: What does 'relevance-based retrieval' primarily aim to achieve?

options.text: Surfacing the stored memories most pertinent to the current situation, rather than everything stored
Deleting all memory immediately upon creation
Storing information with no retrieval capability at all
Making every stored memory exactly the same length

explanation.why_correct: Relevance-based retrieval aims to surface the memories most pertinent to the current situation, as opposed to retrieving everything stored or something unrelated to actual pertinence.

why_incorrect.B: Deleting all memory immediately would eliminate the possibility of ever retrieving anything useful; this is the opposite of effective retrieval.
why_incorrect.C: Storage with no retrieval capability defeats the entire purpose of having long-term memory in the first place.
why_incorrect.D: Uniform memory length has no relationship to whether retrieval surfaces pertinent content for the current need.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Relevance-based retrieval's goal is surfacing the most pertinent stored memories for the current situation, not retrieving everything or nothing.

stem: Why might relying on relevance alone, with no recency consideration, be risky for information that changes over time, such as a user's job title?

options.text: A highly relevant but outdated memory about the old job title might be surfaced as if it still reflects the user's current situation
Job titles never change once recorded, so this is never actually a risk
Relevance and recency are always identical signals with no distinction
This risk only applies to information that never changes

explanation.why_correct: A memory about an old job title remains topically relevant to questions about the user's job, but without recency weighting, it could be surfaced as if it reflects the current situation even though the title has since changed.

why_incorrect.B: Job titles commonly do change over time, which is exactly the kind of changeable information this risk applies to.
why_incorrect.C: Relevance (topical pertinence) and recency (how current the information is) are distinct signals, which is precisely why combining them matters.
why_incorrect.D: This risk specifically applies to information that CAN change over time, like job titles, not information that never changes.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: For information that can change over time, relevance alone risks surfacing an outdated-but-topically-relevant memory as if it reflects the current state.

stem: A meal-planning assistant uses strength-based retention for a low-importance note, 'user once asked about vegan desserts'. Place the events in the order that leads to the note being dropped from the retrieval pool.

options.text: A related query retrieves the note and its strength is boosted
The strength falls below the retention threshold and the note is deprioritized or pruned
The note is written with an initial strength derived from its importance score
Another long idle stretch passes and the strength decays again
Weeks pass with no retrieval and the strength decays

explanation.why_correct: The note starts with an importance-based strength, decays while unused, and is reinforced when a query retrieves it, which pushes it away from the threshold. Further idle time lets decay resume, and only once the strength drops below the retention threshold is the note deprioritized or pruned. Reinforcement therefore delays but does not by itself prevent eventual fading for a low-importance, rarely used memory.
explanation.rule_of_thumb: Write with strength, decay when idle, reinforce on retrieval, decay again, and prune only when the strength crosses the threshold.

stem: An agent's memory system has excellent relevance ranking but no recency weighting and no forgetting mechanism. Over several years of use, what is the most likely cumulative effect?

options.text: An increasing risk of surfacing outdated, superseded information as if it were current, since nothing in the system accounts for staleness or removes clearly outdated content
A guaranteed permanent improvement in retrieval accuracy with no downside
No change at all over time regardless of how much content accumulates
An automatic self-correcting mechanism that fixes all staleness issues without any design effort

explanation.why_correct: Without recency weighting or a forgetting mechanism, accumulated years of content -- including now-outdated facts -- have no mechanism to be deprioritized or removed, increasingly risking outdated information being surfaced as current purely based on topical relevance.

why_incorrect.B: Excellent relevance ranking alone, without recency or forgetting, does not guarantee improving accuracy over time; it specifically risks degrading accuracy as stale content accumulates.
why_incorrect.C: Accumulating years of content, including outdated facts with no mitigation, is very likely to have a real, growing effect on retrieval quality over time.
why_incorrect.D: There is no such automatic self-correcting mechanism; recency weighting and forgetting must be deliberately designed and implemented, not assumed to happen automatically.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Excellent relevance ranking alone, without recency or forgetting, still risks accumulating staleness over time -- all three mechanisms are needed together.

stem: Which scenario best illustrates a contradiction that likely reflects noise or a one-off exception, rather than a genuine update?

options.text: A user who has consistently stated a preference for email over many interactions mentions, just once, in an unusual context, that they'd prefer a phone call for this one specific urgent matter
A user explicitly states, clearly and directly, that they have permanently moved to a new address
A user explicitly and clearly states a permanent change to their name
A user explicitly cancels their account permanently

explanation.why_correct: A single, context-specific request for a phone call for one urgent matter, against a long and consistent pattern of preferring email, looks like a one-off exception tied to that specific situation, not a genuine permanent change to the overall preference.

why_incorrect.B: An explicit, clear statement of a permanent address change is a strong signal of a genuine, intentional update, not noise.
why_incorrect.C: An explicit, clear statement of a permanent name change is a strong signal of a genuine update, not a one-off exception.
why_incorrect.D: An explicit account cancellation is a clear, deliberate action, not an ambiguous one-off exception.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: A single, context-specific deviation from a long-established, consistent pattern is more likely a one-off exception than a genuine permanent update.

stem: Which design choice best supports surfacing the 'most pertinent few' memories rather than everything that loosely matches a query?

options.text: Ranking candidates by a similarity/relevance score and returning only the top few results
Returning every single stored memory regardless of score
Returning results in a completely random order with no ranking at all
Returning results sorted purely alphabetically by their first letter

explanation.why_correct: Scoring candidates by similarity/relevance and returning only the top few directly implements the goal of surfacing the most pertinent memories, rather than everything or an arbitrarily ordered subset.

why_incorrect.B: Returning everything regardless of score is exactly the undifferentiated approach that relevance-based retrieval aims to avoid.
why_incorrect.C: Random ordering with no ranking provides no assurance that the most pertinent memories are actually surfaced.
why_incorrect.D: Alphabetical ordering by first letter has no relationship to actual pertinence or usefulness for the current need.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Ranking by a relevance/similarity score and returning only the top few results is how relevance-based retrieval surfaces the most pertinent content.

stem: A long-running assistant keeps surfacing outdated entries from its memory store. Which TWO mechanisms address this staleness from different angles? (Select TWO)

options.text: Ranking candidates purely by textual similarity to the query
Weighting recency alongside relevance when ranking candidates at retrieval time
Raising the number of retrieved items so current entries are more likely to be included
Removing, deprioritizing, or letting unused low-importance entries decay out of the retrieval pool
Saving each new fact with no link to the older version it replaces

explanation.why_correct: Recency weighting acts at retrieval time by favoring newer information when ranking, while forgetting or decay acts on the store itself by removing or deprioritizing stale entries. They are complementary answers to the same staleness problem.

why_incorrect.A: Similarity-only ranking has no notion of age, so an old entry that matches well can outrank the current one.
why_incorrect.C: Retrieving more items adds more stale and marginal material rather than fixing staleness.
why_incorrect.E: Without a link to the superseded version, nothing signals which entry is current, which makes staleness worse.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Recency fixes staleness at ranking time; forgetting and decay fix it in the store -- use both.

stem: What is the main risk of a memory system that has NO policy at all for handling contradictions, simply storing every version of a fact with no reconciliation?

options.text: The agent may have no clear basis for deciding which version of the fact to actually use, risking inconsistent or confusing behavior
This guarantees the agent will always use the correct version automatically
This approach has no downside of any kind
This eliminates the need for any retrieval mechanism

explanation.why_correct: With no policy to reconcile contradictory stored versions, the agent lacks a clear basis for deciding which version actually reflects reality, risking inconsistent behavior (e.g. sometimes using the old fact, sometimes the new one, with no principled reason).

why_incorrect.B: With no reconciliation policy, there's no mechanism ensuring the correct version is reliably chosen; the choice becomes essentially arbitrary or inconsistent.
why_incorrect.C: This approach has a real, meaningful downside: inconsistent or confusing agent behavior from unresolved contradictions.
why_incorrect.D: A retrieval mechanism is still needed to surface whichever (possibly contradictory) versions are stored; this issue doesn't eliminate that need.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: A memory system with no contradiction-resolution policy risks inconsistent behavior, since there's no principled basis for choosing which stored version reflects reality.
